messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Stress: Stress
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 59-year-old single man who came to the United States from Ghana thirty years ago, and has built a quiet, orderly life as a professor of environmental science at a midwestern university. The traumatic event that shattered his sense of safety did not happen to him directly. It happened to his younger brother, Kofi, during a visit back home five years ago. Kofi was caught in a flash flood while driving home from a market town; his car was swept off a bridge and he drowned. Kwame received the news by phone in his campus office, and he remembers the moment with unbearable clarity: the smell of rain on asphalt drifting through an open window, the sound of his own voice saying "no" over and over, and the certainty that he should have been there to stop it.

In the months that followed, Kwame found himself unable to shake the conviction that he had failed his brother in some fundamental way. He had come to believe that if he had been more attentive to the weather forecasts that week, if he had called Kofi and warned him, Kofi would still be alive. This belief lodged itself in his mind like a splinter, and it began to shape his days. He started checking weather alerts obsessively, sometimes six or seven times an hour, especially whenever he felt even slightly stressed. A difficult faculty meeting, a tense email from a dean, a student's complaint about a grade—any of these would send his hand reaching for his phone, his heart already beginning to pound before he had even looked at the screen.

The connection between stress and his body's alarm system became tighter and tighter. Kwame noticed that his body would react to danger before he had even had time to think. A sudden loud noise in the hallway, a car horn outside his window, a colleague touching his shoulder unexpectedly—each time, his chest would constrict, his palms would sweat, and he would feel a surge of adrenaline that left him shaky and disoriented. He was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. His own living room, with its carefully arranged books and the soft hum of the refrigerator, began to feel charged with threat. He would sit on his couch and find himself scanning the room, listening for running water, for the hiss of a pipe, for any sound that might signal a disaster he had failed to prevent.

Water itself became unbearable. Kwame had always loved the lake near his university, a place he used to walk to between classes. Now he could not go near it. The sight of the still, grey surface, the smell of damp earth and algae, the way the water lapped at the shore—these things would trigger a cascade of images: Kofi's car submerged, the dark current, the helplessness. He began taking longer routes across campus to avoid the lake path. He stopped showering at home, using only quick sponge baths, because the sound of running water in the enclosed space made his throat close. He told himself this was reasonable, that he was simply being careful, but he knew, in the quieter moments, that his life had shrunk around a single, recurring fear.

His work suffered. He cancelled office hours on rainy days. He stopped attending department meetings because the building's basement had flooded once, years ago, and the memory of that damp carpet smell sent him into a panic. He began to avoid stress itself, declining committee assignments, withdrawing from collaborations, letting emails pile up unanswered. He had come to believe that if he could keep his life perfectly still, if he could eliminate every source of pressure, he might also keep the memories at bay. But the opposite was true: the more he avoided, the more vigilant he became. The more vigilant he became, the more triggers he found. Every puddle on the sidewalk, every humid afternoon, every mention of rain in the forecast—each one confirmed that danger was always close, that he could never truly be safe.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was a morning in late spring, when a sudden thunderstorm caught him on his way to campus. He was standing under an awning, watching water pour from the sky, and his body went into full alarm: his vision narrowed, his breath came in gasps, and he was certain, for a terrible moment, that he was going to die. He did not die, but he could not move for twenty minutes afterward. He stood there, soaked and trembling, and for the first time he understood that his vigilance had not protected him. It had only made him a prisoner. He is afraid that if he does not find a way out, he will lose his job, his health, his mind. But what frightens him most is the thought that the only way to stop the fear is to stop caring about Kofi—and that, he is certain, he will never do.
